To improve visibility, we utilize Deep Learning-based image fusion techniques to combine infrared and visible images into a single, unified output. Our novel fusion technique, FIRe-GAN, incorporates Deep Learning to enhance the quality of the fused image, surpassing traditional methods. By integrating cutting-edge Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) into the process, FIRe-GAN effectively mitigates the degradation of the fused images. The performance of FIRe-GAN is evaluated using established metrics such as NIQE, MS-SSIM, and NIQE, which measure the quality of the fused images. The results demonstrate that FIRe-GAN outperforms traditional fusion methods, including DCT, SWT, and LapPyram, as well as other deep learning-based methods like FF-GAN, FDE-GAN, and FIRe-GANw. The efficacy of FIRe-GAN is further validated through its successful application in real-world wildfire scenarios.

This research outlines the process of gathering and analyzing data to identify indicators of depression in social media posts. A custom dataset was created from Twitter by employing a crowdsourcing approach to train and evaluate algorithms capable of detecting depression. The research team also examined the effectiveness of pre-existing algorithms in this domain. The dataset and related research documents, including a link to the Twitter data, are publicly available for further study.

We introduce a stochastic, compartmental, COVID-19 model divided into separate compartments, with each one representing an isolated infectious group, unaffected by others. Each group behaves like a Markov chain, independently, and we derive the long-term behavior of these infected groups as Markov chains having nuclear duals. Our analysis yields explicit expressions for the limit of the transition probability matrices of these groups. Our results hold under the assumption that the basic reproduction number ($R_0$) is less than 1, and as the population size grows indefinitely, the transition matrices converge to matrices containing only the element in the top left corner, which tends towards 1. This implies that as the population size grows, the likelihood that a susceptible individual remains uninfected throughout their lifetime approaches 1.

This research aims to explore the effects of coupling between isoscalar quadrupole and monopole collective motions on the properties of the giant monopole resonance in $^{24}$Mg and $^{28}$Si. By comparing experimental data with results from a microscopic model, the study finds that considering the interaction between these motions leads to an increase in the total energy sum rule and characteristic strength distribution when compared to calculations that neglect this interaction. Moreover, the research demonstrates that the final energy centroid of the resonance is significantly affected by the strength of the coupling between these motions.

This paper examines the stability of biological networks regulated by feedback mechanisms that overcome friction. Our approach involves utilizing a Lyapunov function to demonstrate that temporary oscillations in system dynamics eventually give way to stable convergence, rather than expected limit cycles. Additionally, we explore the effects of parameter changes on stick-slip behavior and present a strategy for avoiding this phenomenon by adjusting system parameters.

A novel framework called Bellman Hedging has been developed to enhance risk-averse reinforcement learning methods by hedging against the most detrimental outcomes. This approach builds upon risk-averse value and policy optimization methods, which can be seen as a more general form of the Maximum Entropy RL. In contrast, Bellman Hedging employs a novel Lagrangian optimization technique to incorporate risk aversion into value optimization, resulting in a self-supervised objective that maintains theoretical guarantees similar to risk-neutral value optimization. Furthermore, Bellman Hedging can be applied to the policy optimization to yield a natural connection to the Maximum Entropy RL and achieve state-of-the-art performance on a variety of MuJoCo tasks.

In the field of sequential recommender systems, researchers have been focusing on developing models that prioritize accurate predictions. However, gaining insights into user motivations behind their item selections remains a relatively underexplored area. To bridge this gap, we introduce a novel approach called HiMo, which integrates a motivation module into the training process to capture users' underlying reasons for making sequential decisions. By training the motivation module alongside the main recurrent encoder, our method can extract and represent the underlying user motivations from both user profiles and sequential interactions. Through comprehensive experiments on three real-world datasets, HiMo demonstrates superior performance in achieving high-precision next-item predictions while also providing interpretable and insightful user motivations.

It is demonstrated that a general class of sources can be integrated into the double confluent Heun equation, which, when considered under the effect of this potential, becomes the transformable DCE. Additionally, a broad method for unfolding these potentials is identified, which is associated with the double confluent Heun spectrum and its symmetric properties.

In the field of data analysis, matrix approximation techniques are widely used to
extract essential information from large datasets.  This paper addresses a critical
aspect of matrix approximation by focusing on its performance under specific real-world
conditions.  We investigate how well these algorithms can recover information from
matrices composed of multiple, diverse components.  We establish fundamental limits
on their ability to accurately reconstruct these matrix parts under various levels of
noise and complexity.  Our analysis reveals that, in some cases, these algorithms
can only converge to a specific boundary condition, rather than a specific value,
when the matrix components are of a specific type.  This phenomenon, known as non-ergodicity,
has significant implications for understanding the limitations of these methods and
their potential applications.

We introduce a novel theoretical framework based on topological models to elucidate the Meissner effect's inherent nature. Our analysis reveals that the Meissner effect arises from a topological deficiency resulting from the absence of gauge symmetry, rather than a deliberate choice to break symmetry. Our theory is built on fundamental principles rather than speculative assumptions, thereby providing a more robust understanding of superconductivity and its relationship with gauge symmetry.

In semi-inclusive $b\to s\ell^+\ell^-$ transitions, a new ratio $R_{semi}$ is proposed, 
which equates to the ratio $R_K$ above $q^2\approx 6$ GeV$^2$ and to $R_{J/\psi}$ 
at low $q^2$. The new ratio is evaluated using a binned analysis based on 
experimental data and theoretical predictions, revealing consistency with the Standard Model.

This paper presents a decentralized architecture and distributed control approach for linear multi-channel systems, which is characterized by a unique combination of full-spectrum stability, adaptability, and efficiency.  The proposed structure is flexible, allowing for the inclusion of a relatively small number of parameters for stability in the regulatory process, which also maintains computational efficiency, specifically polynomial complexity, based on the number of subsystems in the network, while the regulatory controller can be easily updated by adding or removing subsystems without requiring a complete redesign of the system.  The proposed distributed approach is built upon an innovative application of the Kalman filter, which is designed to be resilient to uncertainty, and also offers an alternative to the traditional model-based control methods, which often suffer from rigidity and complexity in the regulatory process.  The proposed architecture is shown to have a unique combination of properties, which includes the ability to achieve a stable and efficient regulatory process, as well as the ability to adapt to changes in the system, and also offers a range of new insights into the design of decentralized controllers and their performance, which also includes the ability to achieve a stable and efficient regulatory process, and also offers a range of new insights into the design of decentralized controllers and their performance.  The proposed architecture is shown to have a unique combination of properties, which includes the ability to achieve a stable and efficient regulatory process, and also offers a range of new insights into the design of decentralized controllers and their performance.

The COVID-19 pandemic has had a profound impact on the world, with the primary focus on detecting and classifying the disease. Given the vast number of patients, healthcare professionals face significant challenges in diagnosing and treating them efficiently. Radiologists, in particular, are tasked with examining numerous chest CT scans, which can be overwhelming given the current situation. To address this issue, researchers have developed automated COVID-19 detection systems using deep learning-based computer-aided diagnosis. However, these systems have primarily focused on classifying scans as positive or negative, overlooking the varying stages of COVID-19. To bridge this gap, researchers have proposed a dual-stage COVID-19 categorization framework that classifies scans into positive, negative, and three COVID-19 severity stages. By leveraging the power of BERT, this system can extract semantic features from medical reports and classify scans more accurately. To further enhance classification, researchers have proposed using attention mechanisms to identify the most important words in medical reports. To test the effectiveness of this framework, researchers have conducted experiments using the COVID-19 database and achieved significant results.

Network science encompasses various topics, including researchers from different backgrounds, such as those studying social networks and those analyzing the internet's network topology. To effectively collaborate and exchange findings, researchers need a common language and framework. To this end, we have developed a comprehensive atlas that outlines the key concepts and tools of network science, enabling seamless communication and collaboration among researchers. The atlas provides detailed explanations of fundamental topics, such as network construction and analysis, and more advanced subjects, such as studying temporal and multiplex networks. By categorizing its content into distinct areas, such as a dictionary of key terms and a curated list of essential software tools, the atlas serves as a valuable resource for both novice and experienced network researchers.

The study of eco-evolutionary dynamics has expanded from examining the evolution of a single species to analyzing the complex interactions between multiple species and their environments.  This introduction to eco-evolutionary dynamics draws on a variety of concepts from evolutionary theory, including adaptation, evolutionary traps, and rapid evolution, to explain how and why these interactions occur.  By incorporating ideas such as eco-evolutionary feedback loops and shifting basins, the text explores how the interplay between ecological and evolutionary processes can lead to diverse outcomes, including cycles, stability, and instability.  The text also highlights the importance of timescales and modulators in shaping eco-evolutionary dynamics, and how these factors can influence the emergence of new traits and behaviors.  Overall, the text provides a comprehensive framework for understanding the complex and dynamic nature of eco-evolutionary systems, and how these interactions shape the living world.

Self-supervised learning methods for speech have been developed to improve speech representation without the need for manual labeling. These techniques, however, have a notable weakness: their effectiveness can be severely compromised by the presence of non-target audio input, such as background noise or irrelevant speech. This vulnerability poses a significant challenge to their application in real-world scenarios. To address this issue, researchers have created an open-source platform for evaluating the susceptibility of self-supervised learning models to hostile environments. This platform enables researchers to systematically investigate how different types of non-target audio affect self-supervised learning models and how this impact varies across different tasks.

The rise of the Internet enabled decentralized platforms, such as Dropbox, Google Drive, and OneDrive, to revolutionize file sharing.  A similar phenomenon is now taking place with decentralized marketplaces, such as Amazon, eBay, and Alibaba, being transformed by the integration of blockchain technology.  This fusion enables a truly decentralized marketplace where goods and services can be traded without the need for a central intermediary.  This research paper delves into the key components of such a decentralized marketplace and its underlying blockchain infrastructure.  It also explores the advantages and disadvantages of such a decentralized marketplace, as well as its potential to disrupt traditional markets.

E-values are utilized to gauge the magnitude of unaccounted non-random data missingness. We have developed a novel method for evaluating the potential impact on research findings by using E-values in place of traditional multiple imputation sensitivity approaches. The process involves creating a Bayesian imputation model and quantifying the influence of a specific non-random missingness parameter, denoted as theta, on outcome estimates. By utilizing a prior distribution for theta, we can calculate the posterior probability of it exceeding a chosen threshold, known as the reverse missingness proportion (RMP) probability. We have also devised a new metric called the reverse missingness proportion probability ratio (RMP ratio) to compare results with and without a particular exposure. This approach is illustrated through two case studies: a clinical trial assessing the effect of an intervention on mortality and an observational study examining the effect of an exposure on mortality.

The quantum plane, defined by the equation $xy=yx_q$, comprises all the commutative relationships within the algebra $\mathbb{C}\left\langle x,y\right\rangle_q$. This study delves into the specific characteristics of a particular subgroup, denoted as $\mathbb{S}$, which preserves the quantum plane under the given relationship $xy=yx_q$. In contrast to previously established knowledge, which categorized a broader class of transformations that extend beyond the quantum plane, we establish a comprehensive list of symmetries associated with the Drinfeld double $D\left(U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)\right)$ and identify novel finite-dimensional representations of this algebraic structure.

Federated learning has become a prominent approach for training machine learning models in the Internet of Vehicles (IoV) domain. This method leverages local data stored on vehicles to train models, eliminating the need to transfer sensitive data to a central server. However, the challenge of ensuring data security and privacy arises, particularly when vehicles communicate with a central server. A promising solution to this problem involves integrating blockchain technology, which provides robust security features such as data integrity, traceability, and decentralization. This paper provides an in-depth analysis of existing research on security and privacy solutions within the blockchain-federated learning framework in IoV, highlighting the various challenges and proposed solutions. A comprehensive taxonomy is also introduced to categorize these solutions, and an extensive literature review reveals a total of 21 relevant studies addressing blockchain-based data security and privacy challenges in federated learning. This review aims to offer valuable insights for researchers and developers working on ensuring secure and private data communication within the IoV domain.

The ALICE experiment at the LHC has gathered beauty and charm production data in central pp collisions at 5.02 TeV. By analyzing the decay of beauty and charm particles into muons and pions, the cross-sections for both prompt and semi-prompt production of D0, D+, and J/psi mesons have been calculated. These findings are compared to theoretical models and previous measurements, including the ALICE beauty production measurement at 7 TeV.

The advancement of quantum computing has been significantly propelled by the development of superconducting circuits, a field that has been explored by researchers at Fermilab and Argonne National Laboratory for over a decade. The lab has established an artificial environment resembling outer space, characterized by its ultra-high vacuum and cryogenic capabilities, to facilitate quantum computing experiments. The facility, known as the Millikelvin Platform, is equipped with 12 custom-built dilution refrigerators and offers a range of services, including state-of-the-art cryogenic and beamline services, to support a diverse range of experiments. The platform's capabilities have been utilized by numerous experiments, including those conducted by researchers at Fermilab and Argonne, to advance the frontiers of quantum computing.

This study examines real-world instances of compromised cryptography in cryptographic libraries implemented using Python. Our investigation centers on four prevalent issues: the utilization of outdated, insecure hashing algorithms; the use of unsalted or weakly salted password hashing; the use of obsolete encryption standards; and the use of poorly managed randomly generated keys. To address these issues, we developed a static analysis tool, CryptoPy, which identifies these vulnerabilities. We applied this tool to a repository containing 500 open-source Python projects and discovered 150 instances of compromised cryptography. Notably, our findings reveal that the use of improperly managed random key generation is a relatively uncommon issue, whereas the other three issues are pervasive.

This paper introduces a straightforward yet efficient method for generating large-scale, diverse training data for vision-based algorithms, such as those used in autonomous vehicles. Our approach leverages human labeling tools to create a vast dataset with minimal manual input. The core of our method involves leveraging human ability to correct algorithmic errors, enabling us to produce a substantial amount of high-quality data with significantly reduced human effort. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method by using the generated data to train and evaluate vision-based driving algorithms, specifically for two challenging tasks: correcting camera misalignment and detecting and correcting lane markings. Our experiments show that the proposed method yields state-of-the-art results, outperforming existing solutions.

This study introduces a new reconstruction approach called NuSPAN, a network-based method that leverages the proximal mean network to handle sparse, nonuniform data. Proximal networks are designed to solve optimization problems that are common in network reconstruction, and the proposed method uses a proximal mean node to generate a sparse, nonuniform output. To achieve this, a special output layer called SNODE is developed, which combines a sparse nonuniform Fourier transform and a node selection process. The effectiveness of NuSPAN is demonstrated through its application in reconstructuring seismic reflectivity from undersampled data.

This study delves into the investigation of semigroups of composition operators on BMOA-type spaces defined by the norm:
$$
\sup_{z\in\mathbb{D}}\Big|\int_0^{2\pi}f'(z e^{it})e^{-it}dt\Big|^{1/p},
$$
where $0<p<\infty$. We derive sufficient conditions ensuring that the semigroup of composition operators remains bounded within the space, and further, this research provides the norm estimate of the semigroup.

We have developed a novel technique to determine critical scaling operators and their correlation lengths in two-dimensional critical systems with non-unitary symmetry, utilizing wavefunction simulations. This approach relies on comparing wavefunctions from the same quantum state expressed in different bases to extract wavefunction overlaps. By applying the technique, we can identify the eigenvalues of the transfer matrix, thereby obtaining the scaling dimensions of relevant operators. Furthermore, we can obtain critical scaling operators and their correlation lengths, which enables us to calculate universal finite-size corrections for specific physical observables. By employing this technique, we have computed the ground state energy of the Haagerup model on various lattices, thereby deriving the universal finite-size corrections for this system. Our analysis also reveals that the ground state energy converges to a specific value, which is consistent with predictions made using the Reshetikhin-Turaev invariant of three-sphere manifolds.

We introduce a novel approach, POStagger, that tackles the challenges of historical language variation by predicting a set of possible part-of-speech labels instead of relying on single labels. This method allows for more accurate and reliable predictions, particularly in cases where annotators disagree on labels. By utilizing ensemble models and incorporating prediction intervals, POStagger achieves better performance on modern and historical corpora alike. Our experiments demonstrate that POStagger can deliver more trustworthy predictions, and it offers greater flexibility in retrieving desired labels, which can be particularly useful in scenarios where confidence is low.

This paper delves into an alternative formulation of $L^1$-convergence in measure that is not subject to uniform integrability constraints. By establishing a space of functions that is not uniformly integrable but still $L^1$-convergent in measure, we develop a convergence theorem analogous to the Dominated Convergence Theorem. The underlying proof leverages a generalized version of Fubini's Theorem that extends to products of multiple measurable spaces.

We introduce a knowledge-based system that converts requirements for urban development into formal logical statements. This conversion facilitates the utilization of existing model-based tools in urban planning. This system is designed to handle requirements specified using the CReq language, a purpose-built notation for city-related needs. This notation is structured to capture fundamental aspects of cities, such as their geography, inhabitants, and organizational entities. This paper outlines the CReq notation, presents a model for city structure, and demonstrates how to translate CReq statements into SMT formulas. This demonstration is based on cities defined using the recent Open City Database standard.

A quantum code based on concealed inverses is explored for correcting errors in quantum computations.
This code, established over a quantum ring-network, is implemented using superconducting qubits.
Initially, a quantum error is identified on any qubit within the network.
Subsequently, the error is effectively neutralized through interaction with neighboring qubits within the code.
This code, consisting of multiple qubits, is found to be effective in eliminating errors affecting up to (n-1) qubits.
Furthermore, the code is found to be effective in eliminating errors affecting (n-1) qubits out of a network containing (2n-1) qubits.
This is demonstrated by a quantum code with five qubits, which is capable of correcting errors affecting up to four qubits.
This is achieved by implementing the quantum code on a quantum chip, which is a crucial step towards the development of fault-tolerant quantum computation.

We demonstrate that in regular categories with finite coproducts, any preorder can be visually represented as a pair of functors that form a bicartesian morphism. Furthermore, an equivalence relation within such categories can be depicted through a similar bicartesian depiction, consisting of two morphisms that form a product.

To better prepare for extreme weather conditions at sea, such as storms, hurricanes, and typhoons, it's crucial to understand how multiple ocean parameters like wave height, direction, and period interact during extreme events. This study proposes a statistical model that can forecast joint ocean states given specific weather conditions, and it's validated using real-world data from three major storms in the Atlantic, Pacific, and Indian oceans. The results show that forecasting ocean conditions based on weather data can significantly improve maritime safety and navigation.

Recent advancements in vision-language models have led to promising results in various visual tasks by leveraging next-token prediction. However, these models' text and image understanding capabilities are often mutually exclusive, and their reliance on unannotated data can lead to text bias. To address these limitations, we introduce VT-CLIP, a new model that integrates image captions to enhance text understanding. By incorporating a novel visual-assisted token and employing an image-caption alignment strategy, VT-CLIP achieves superior performance on a range of tasks, including zero-shot classification, image retrieval, and web captioning, outperforming current state-of-the-art models.

We suggest an approach to tackle the task of assigning a label to an operator by utilizing only limited information about it, where the given data is an operator matrix. This approach is unique in that it doesn't rely on the underlying assumptions of an operator Hilbert space. Instead, our method focuses on the fundamental property of an operator matrix, where each entry has a bounded norm. This leads to the creation of a universal noisy matrix framework that is applicable to a wide range of operator matrices. Within this framework, we establish the existence of a unique optimal labeling strategy, where the label is determined by the geometric characteristics of the matrix. This, in turn, enables us to establish a connection between the given data and the true operator matrix, and establish a bound on the error of the labeling process.

We identify the segments of the quaternionic Eilenberg-Mac Lane spectra in categories of 8-graded super abelian groups and super $\mathbb{Z}/8\mathbb{Z}$-modules, extending previous work on the construction of spectra in these categories.

In this study, we establish the concept of tight Hilbert polynomial, which we then employ to examine the local rings that are robust in Foxby's sense. We demonstrate that a complete intersection local ring is invariant under Foxby's operations, and for other non-Foxby-invariant rings, we provide a method to calculate their tight Hilbert polynomial and examine how this polynomial behaves in relation to Foxby-by-Faulhaber operations.

Radiologists and pathologists utilize digital imaging to identify, locate, and measure abnormalities in clinical samples. To optimize their workflow, they utilize AI-powered tools that support diagnostic and grading processes. These tools generate outcomes in various formats, often tailored to specific imaging modalities and applications. This incompatibility poses challenges for cross-institutional research and limits the practical application of AI models. To address this issue, we present Highdicom, a Python-based library that standardizes the representation of image-based analysis results across various fields of radiology and pathology. Highdicom adheres to established medical standards, including DICOM, HL7, and high-level medical guidelines. By doing so, it facilitates seamless exchange of analysis results between institutions and enables researchers to efficiently deploy their AI models on clinical imaging data from different sources. Highdicom provides a comprehensive set of tools for creating and parsing standardized input and output data, enabling the development of AI models that can be easily transferred between different environments.

A detailed analysis of the Einstein-Hilbert action's variation is carried out, separating the bulk and surface terms to derive the Noether charge of the bulk term, which yields the Virasoro algebra. This process reveals that the surface term's variation is linked to the bulk and does not produce a corresponding algebra, supporting a previous hypothesis. Additionally, the study investigates the role of the surface term in the black hole entropy derivation from the Noether charge, discovering that the surface term contributes to the bulk under specific conditions, which can be likened to a disorder in the bulk. Ultimately, the study presents a new formula for the total Noether charge, incorporating both bulk and surface terms.

Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have significantly improved the accuracy of predicting DNA sequences, yet most existing models heavily rely on sequence alignment, a method that is labor-intensive and prone to errors. To address this limitation, we have developed an unsupervised representation learning approach that enables the extraction of DNA patterns solely from raw sequences. By utilizing a combination of convolutional neural networks and Word2Vec, our model can effectively learn meaningful DNA representations without the need for sequences to be pre-aligned. Furthermore, we have created a novel neural network architecture, dubbed DNANet, which incorporates our proposed framework and demonstrates superior performance in predicting DNA sequences, particularly in tasks involving gene function prediction and variant effect assessment.

This research explores the Clebsch authorization of Lie-Poisson systems derived from Euler-Poincaré equations on a semidirect sum Lie algebra. We specifically examine applications to ideal magnetohydrodynamics and invariant metrics on groups. We demonstrate that a Lie-Poisson system can be factored into two parts, one of which corresponds to Euler-Poincaré equations, while the other represents a Poisson bracket for the remaining variables. We further investigate the involution properties of a particular set of Casimirs, yielding a modified Euler-Lagrange variational principle for the original Clebsch authorized system.

Our study is based on a sample of 1,114 eccentric planets that were identified from the Kepler light curves, which were analyzed in six papers. We have found that the distribution of eccentricities in this sample is similar to that of planets in irregular orbits detected by the KMTNet survey.
