Recent advancements in representation learning have led to the development of
powerful techniques capable of producing high-quality models, yet these models
are susceptible to significant performance degradation when faced with minor
variations. To address this limitation, our research introduces the Deep Optimal
Regularization (DOR) method, which integrates hierarchical regularizers based on
Sinkhorn distances to enhance robustness and generalization capabilities. The
DOR approach effectively combines deep, intermediate, and surface-level
regularizers to regulate the distribution of training data, and our experiments
demonstrate that incorporating all three levels of regularization yields the most
effective results. Notably, our findings reveal that the traditional use of
regularizers as supplementary tools to minimize overfitting can be reinterpreted
as a means of representation enhancement, and that the primary advantage of the
DOR approach lies in its ability to generate high-quality models rather than
merely reducing overfitting.

The widespread use of contact tracing apps in various countries has been met with significant skepticism due to concerns over data sharing and the overall efficacy of tracing within communities. In the UK, the government's decision to limit data exchange between contact tracing services in communities with fewer than 10,000 tested individuals led to local authorities creating their own tracing systems, resulting in varying levels of coverage and the need to assess the impact of this fragmentation on overall tracing effectiveness. A study was conducted to evaluate the local and cross-border impact of these collaborations on the overall efficacy of contact tracing in England, using the "EpiFit" model to simulate the spread of SARS-CoV-2 and the impact of contact tracing. The results showed that contact tracing coverage and community R values were relatively resilient to fragmentation, with the optimal level of coverage being around 60%, and the community R values dropping significantly below 1 when coverage exceeded 50%. The study also highlighted the importance of regular data sharing between different tracing services to maintain high levels of coverage and the overall efficacy of contact tracing.

Our investigation of the Melotte 72 open cluster, located at a distance of 1.23 kpc, reveals an age of 1.05 Gyr.  Observations indicate that this cluster exhibits significant chemical variations, displaying a pattern of metallicity versus alpha element ratio that differs from other clusters.  The cluster's members show a split in carbon and nitrogen content, with a separation that surpasses that of clusters with a similar age and metallicity.  Furthermore, our analysis indicates that Melotte 72's properties are more aligned with those of clusters that experienced a single burst of star formation, rather than those that experienced multiple bursts.

The topology of randomly perturbed trajectories in holomorphic vector fields on complex projective space has been studied, particularly the distribution of Betti numbers for paths following a specified homology class. In a recent study, this was extended to the case of large dimensions and specific vector fields with sparse connections, yielding precise predictions for Betti number distributions and demonstrating that lower-order Betti numbers have Gaussian patterns.

Robotic systems with multiple cameras can greatly enhance performance, but they often require precise calibration, a task that can be time-consuming and labor-intensive. In this paper, we present an innovative approach to calibrating eye-in-Hand cameras by leveraging the information contained within images captured by said cameras. Our method, named SingleIEH, uniquely automates calibrations by learning from a single image, thereby eliminating the need for additional, unimaged cameras or controlled environments. To validate the effectiveness of our approach, we developed a novel dataset consisting of images taken during robotic manipulations, and demonstrate its utility by successfully applying it to both simulated and real robotic systems.

A widely accepted method in robot learning is reinforcement learning, a form of trial-and-error learning.  However, a significant challenge arises when training robots to perform complex tasks, as their unintended movements can lead to negative rewards.  To address this issue, we introduce an inverse reinforcement learning approach, where the robot learns to avoid restricted regions of its state-action space.  We call this method Reverse Constrained Reinforcement Learning, abbreviated as RCRL.  In contrast to traditional reinforcement learning, RCRL focuses on the transitions between states, rather than the states themselves.  We propose two methods for defining the restricted regions: one based on a fixed hyperplane and another using a half-plane.  Our experimental results demonstrate that RCRL outperforms traditional reinforcement learning in solving complex tasks, as it enables the robot to navigate around restricted regions.

The GAIA space telescope launched in 2013 is revolutionizing our understanding of the Milky Way galaxy. With its unique capabilities, GAIA is creating an unprecedented map of the galaxy's structure, allowing scientists to study its past and predict its future. By collecting data on the positions, movements, brightness, and chemical properties of the galaxy, GAIA is providing valuable insights into the formation and evolution of the Milky Way. This paper provides an overview of GAIA's scientific objectives and the groundbreaking discoveries it has made so far.

We have developed an efficient tool for identifying treewidth in small graph areas, building on previous work that introduced a planar graph algorithm for treewidth detection. Our extension allows the tool to handle non-planar graphs and, in addition, generates near-optimal tree decompositions within localized graph representations. The method relies on pre-existing tree decompositions and efficiently incorporates them into the final tree structure.

Network analysis is a widely used method for examining relationships between entities, such as genes, species, or individuals. The versatility of network analysis stems from its ability to capture various relationship types, which can be represented through weighted networks. However, the interpretation of these weights is often unclear, leading to inconsistent interpretations across different domains. This study aims to clarify the meaning of weighted network weights by focusing on the heterogeneity of relationship types and the distinction between observed and inferred networks. By examining the statistical properties of network weights, we provide a framework for understanding and comparing weights within and between networks. Our framework highlights the importance of considering the distribution of relationship types and the methods used to estimate weights. We also discuss the impact of network sparsity and the trade-offs between sensitivity and specificity in network inference. Ultimately, our work provides a foundation for the development of new network metrics and methods that can accommodate diverse relationship types and measurements.

Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) are a promising method for solving complex partial differential equations that arise in various scientific and engineering applications. However, PINNs can be susceptible to inaccuracies due to limitations in data availability and optimization techniques. To address these challenges, we developed a technique for assessing the reliability of PINNs after solving an equation. Our approach involves analyzing the optimization process to develop a metric for estimating the potential errors in the solution, enabling informed decision-making about when additional computational resources should be allocated to improve accuracy.

Air pollution and infectious diseases have a long-standing connection, with research indicating that exposure to particulate matter and air pollutants can contribute to the spread and severity of viral infections. The effects are observed at both the individual and population levels, with increased risk of infection and more severe outcomes for those exposed to air pollution. The COVID-19 pandemic has accelerated research into the relationship between air pollution and viral transmission, utilizing geostatistical models and advanced machine learning algorithms to analyze the correlation between air quality and infection rates. The integration of these technologies into atmospheric contamination models has enabled researchers to gain deeper insights into the complex dynamics of infectious disease transmission and inform public health policies.

To differentiate between zero bias peaks arising from either unconventional superconductivity or from zero energy Majorana modes, we suggest performing tunneling spectroscopy with an ohmically damped junction. Unlike the commonly used high impedance electrodes, our proposed setup involves a resistive electrode and can effectively filter out zero bias peaks not originating from Majorana modes. The sensitivity of the setup to these non-Majorana peaks can be adjusted by changing the channel length.

We examine a diverse action set linear bandit problem, where each arm has a limited and distinct set of actions. The bandit's goal is to maximize the reward for each unique action across all arms. This scenario is prevalent in real-world applications, such as optimizing content recommendations on social media platforms. The challenge of identifying the best action within each arm becomes a crucial step in achieving overall success. To address this issue, we introduce the concept of common and individual arm means. The arm common mean represents the average of all unique action means, whereas individual arm means represent the mean of specific action values. The primary objective of this study is to minimize regret by achieving two key goals: first, to identify the best arm efficiently based on arm common mean; second, to determine the mean of each unique action within the arm. To achieve this, we introduce the Diversified Linear Bandit (Diversified Bandit for short), a novel algorithm. The Diversified Bandit is designed to balance exploration and exploitation, allowing it to identify the best arm efficiently. Additionally, it employs individual arm mean estimation to determine the mean of each unique action within the arm. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that the Diversified Bandit achieves a logarithmic regret bound, thereby establishing its efficiency. The results of our experiments with the algorithm on real-world datasets show its effectiveness in addressing the issue.

Graphene exhibits a unique combination of massless Dirac fermions and exceptional valley degrees of freedom, which, when combined, can lead to the emergence of quantum Hall effects associated with valleys. This unique property allows for the development of devices capable of detecting and manipulating valley currents. However, existing proposals for valley Hall effect devices have yet to be realized experimentally. In this study, we propose an alternative approach to generate a valley current by leveraging the orbital Hall effect in graphene with an intrinsic gap. This effect can be understood as a more accurate description of the valley Hall effect in this context. By carefully engineering the orbital Hall effect, we can create devices that facilitate the efficient injection and detection of valley currents.

The effectiveness of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) is increasingly being utilized in various applications, but their vulnerability to data manipulation poses a significant threat. To address this concern, we introduce a reinforcement learning framework that enables GNNs to engage in adversarial interactions with graphs, thereby simulating adversarial attacks. This framework allows the GNN to optimize its performance by strategically making decisions based on its own predictions. Through reconfiguring its internal architecture, the GNN can effectively defend itself against adversarial attacks. Our proposed framework is demonstrated on both Link Prediction and Node Classification tasks, and it is shown that the model can successfully adapt its structure to mitigate the effects of adversarial attacks.

To improve the accuracy of stellar catalog matching, we developed a novel photometric approach that complements traditional astrometry-based matching methods. By integrating astrometry and star colors, we created a combined metric to facilitate more precise cross-referencing of stellar catalogs. This enhanced method was successfully applied to two datasets, yielding significant results. Firstly, we matched the Gaia EDR3 and 2MASS catalogs to identify corresponding stellar pairs, allowing us to calculate the distance modulus between them. The distribution of distance moduli for these pairs aligns well with the expected values, demonstrating the efficacy of our method. Secondly, we matched the Gaia EDR3 and APOGEE-2N catalogs to calculate the distance of each APOGEE-2N star and compare them with the distances derived from other methods. The agreement between our results and other methods highlights the reliability of our method. Overall, our approach successfully leverages astrometry and star colors to enhance cross-referencing of stellar catalogs, providing valuable insights into stellar properties and distances.

A minimal edge cover of a hypergraph is defined as a collection of edges, such that every vertex in the hypergraph is contained within at least one edge, and removing any edge results in a failure to cover all vertices. In our investigation, we examine the properties of infinite minimal edge covers in the context of hypergraphs. We establish that for hypergraphs with maximum edge size k, the minimal edge covers always contain a common element if the edge size k is finite and less than the infinite cardinality $\aleph_0$. Furthermore, for infinite edge covers, we demonstrate a scenario where the minimal edge covers can be restricted to a set of size less than the first uncountable cardinality. We also explore the implications of our findings in the context of graph coloring, specifically for countably infinite graphs, by showing that certain large sets of vertices can be colored with a single color, resulting in the existence of a cycle of length k for all k greater than 2.

Domain knowledge representation relies heavily on graphs and relationships, which are often visualized using trees, limiting their applicability to hierarchical structures. However, real-world data frequently involves complex, non-hierarchical connections. To address this challenge, OntoPlot, a novel visualization technique, has been developed to effectively display large-scale, complex graphs. OntoPlot employs a hybrid visualization approach, combining plot-based and tree-based visualizations, which facilitates the effective navigation and exploration of both the global structure and detailed information within the graph. By incorporating interactive features, OntoPlot enhances user experience and enables seamless navigation. An extensive usability study involving 15 participants demonstrated the superiority of OntoPlot over traditional tree-based visualizations, revealing its significant benefits in identifying and navigating relationships within large graphs.

This paper presents an innovative approach to semi-supervised end-to-end automatic speech recognition (RNN-T). The proposed method leverages the potential of generative models to facilitate cross-dataset distribution learning, which can enhance ASR performance. We introduce C2GAN, a modified version of CycleGAN, that enables the distribution of two datasets to be transformed into one another. In addition, another technique is introduced, which involves swapping the loss values of the training data and validation data, respectively. The experimental results demonstrate that the C2GAN approach, combined inter-domain penalties, outperforms the baseline model, yielding a significant 1.5% absolute improvement in the word error rate on the Switchboard dataset.

A key characteristic of life is the ability to navigate autonomously, which robots also need to accomplish to interact effectively with their surroundings. This study focuses on enabling robots to independently move in familiar environments, employing a predictive approach that allows them to anticipate their movements' outcomes. This strategy reduces the search space for optimal navigation paths, streamlining the process. This method is particularly suitable for robots with fixed propulsion, demonstrating its potential through successful tests in a real-world warehouse setting.

Our research reveals that the Soret effect in soft molecules is significantly influenced by their internal freedom of movement. Through molecular dynamics simulations, we observed that increased flexibility in side chains leads to a more pronounced separation of hot and cold regions. This phenomenon is attributed to varying densities of soft molecules, which are a result of the competition between thermal kinetic energy and the energy required for the reconfiguration of their structures. Consequently, the Soret effect is amplified due to the asymmetric diffusion rates of different molecular components.

Recent advancements in neural composition models have been substantial, 
particularly with the integration of the highly effective transformer architecture. 
Despite the growing interest in evaluating these systems, existing evaluation 
metrics have been found to be unreliable, often failing to accurately reflect the 
quality of the generated output. Our research introduces a cutting-edge 
evaluation method that leverages the capabilities of the transformer architecture, 
utilizing state-of the-art pre-trained models to create a highly accurate and 
reliable evaluation metric. This innovative approach, known as effective 
transformer similarity, demonstrates superior performance on various datasets 
compared to the established ROUGE metric, showcasing remarkable consistency and 
accuracy in evaluating neural composition systems.

In practical applications of pedestrian identification, the issue of false positives is a significant challenge. The limitation of traditional methods to produce a single score per pair of bounding boxes is a key factor contributing to this problem. To overcome this limitation, we have developed an innovative approach called box re-ranking that utilizes embedding features to jointly identify pedestrian instances and their corresponding detection boxes. This approach is unique in its ability to leverage detection and re-identification data simultaneously, but it is susceptible to errors stemming from detection inaccuracies. To mitigate this issue, we have incorporated unsupervised domain adaptation techniques to improve the robustness of the method against such errors. Experimental results on two real-world datasets demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on challenging scenarios involving domain shifts, and further analysis reveals that it effectively reduces the occurrence of false positives.

This paper examines the potential of using visual representation and vocoding techniques to enhance audio quality. Our research indicates that converting audio into a visual format and then back to its original form can yield improved results. Furthermore, we demonstrate how these refined audio signals can be further refined using analysis-synthesis vocoding, effectively removing distortions and noise. Our experiments with different models and datasets, such as the WSJ and LibriSpeech, show that this approach can significantly boost word error rates and overall performance.

Our ability to accurately throw objects to a designated target is a crucial skill.
This accuracy relies heavily on the correct execution of the throwing motion,
specifically the point of release. In this study, we examine the effects of releasing
an object prematurely or delaying its release on its trajectory and final destination.
By analyzing these scenarios, we aim to uncover the underlying principles that enable
us to throw objects with such precision.

Recent advancements in Neural Machine Translation (NMT) have led to impressive results, but imperfect translations of complex sentences persist. To address this, we introduce a novel approach decoupling NMT into two interconnected tasks: translating individual sentence components and identifying the sentence's syntactic structure. By separating these tasks, decoders can leverage the rich information contained in syntax, and our experiments demonstrate that this strategy surpasses conventional methods. Furthermore, decoders can utilize various syntactic representations, and empirical evidence shows that link-style representations are particularly effective.

A comprehensive database, the Binding Energy Assessment Platform, is introduced, which contains quantum chemical binding energy data for 1173 species pairs, sourced from 101 publications. This database is designed to support astrochemical research and is accompanied by a visualisation tool that enables users to explore the data interactively. Our analysis reveals that hydrogen-containing species tend to exhibit broader binding energy ranges compared to non-hydrogen-containing species. Furthermore, we found that binding energy values for species involving hydrogen are generally higher than those not involving hydrogen.

A stochastic multiplicative process is analyzed, with its minimum value dynamically dependent on the sample size and progressively converging to a predetermined value as it increases. The statistical properties of this process are studied, with a particular focus on the distribution of its maximum absolute value. The findings are then compared to simulations, demonstrating a satisfactory match. The statistical properties derived can potentially be utilized to identify power-law distributions that are truncated in a specific manner.

We introduce a novel approach called shallow shades, which employs Clifford circuits to evaluate quantum devices' capabilities in executing complex algorithms. By utilizing random Clifford circuits, we can create a benchmark that balances between being easily solvable through approximate eigenvector projection and being too close to classical capabilities. Our method, shallow shades, involves analyzing the outcomes of Clifford circuits with low noise and limited depth, thereby offering a more accurate reflection of quantum devices' capabilities. Furthermore, we demonstrate that shallow shades can be extended to assess the capabilities of variational quantum algorithms, thereby providing a more comprehensive benchmarking framework.

The reflection coefficient's $|k|$ behavior at infinity for the Davey-Stewartson II equations was studied, with specific equations given for both positive and negative $\delta$. However, earlier studies had a limitation in fully determining the leading-order asymptotic behavior for $-\delta$ cases, prompting the current investigation to derive precise estimates for the diagonal R-matrix and ultimately the reflection coefficient's behavior, particularly in terms of its phase.

A text categorization issue is often addressed by training a classifier on labeled data. However, the data may contain anomalies that affect the classifier's performance. To counter this effect, researchers have developed methods to enhance the robustness of classifiers against such distortions. This paper presents two new variants of modifications, known as Sibylvariant modifications, that impact only the classification of test samples. The first variant involves adjusting the decision boundary to favor a particular category. The second variant involves assigning varying levels of importance to each class. The robustness of these modifications is demonstrated through theoretical analysis and empirical testing. The study reveals that Sibylvariant modifications outperform existing methods in scenarios where the type of modification is unknown.

We introduce a new method that teaches machines to generate understandable linear representations of complex concepts, based on their ability to explain their own reasoning. By using data from the GPT-2 model, we show that a linear visualization of the model's knowledge can be both human-interpretable and effective in guiding the learning process. Our model produces training data that allows human observers to see how the visualization evolves, and we find that adding this guidance improves learning in complex tasks. Additionally, we develop a novel linear visualization format and create a tool to automatically generate it from the model's internal representations.

This study investigates the impact of model pruning and quantization on improving machine translation for languages with limited resources. We analyzed four different models, including two that were optimized using Low-Bit quantization and two that were pruned through quantization and then retrained with pruning-based methods. When compared to the original models, the modified models demonstrated improved accuracy and robustness, particularly after being retrained. Notably, the smallest model achieved a remarkable 50% reduction in parameters while only experiencing a 1.5% decline in translation accuracy.

By examining the Euler-Lagrange hyperequation hypergraph, we develop a novel Lagrangian hypergraph density matrix, whose corresponding Euler-Lagrange hyperequation hypergraph inherently embodies the maximum action principle principle. The newly introduced density matrix exhibits a solitary nature, facilitating its application to the theoretical modeling of solitary waves in hypergraph systems.

The detection of pneumonia in chest CT scans is a significant challenge in the medical field, particularly due to the scarcity of high-quality data. To overcome this limitation, researchers have developed a semi-supervised learning approach that utilizes a novel graph convolutional network to improve the accuracy of pneumonia segmentation. By employing a self-supervised learning strategy, the proposed method efficiently reduces the amount of training data required. Furthermore, a data augmentation technique has been implemented to enhance the robustness of the model. The results demonstrate that this approach achieves better performance than existing methods, particularly when working with limited data.

Current image description models excel at generating detailed descriptions, 
described by vivid and descriptive language. Nonetheless, they often overlook
the user's preference for the level of detail required. We propose a new
Regulated Image Description (RID) task that enables users to control the
amount of detail in the description. To achieve this, we introduce a 3-level
classification system and a corresponding P3 prompt template. The system can 
be easily adapted to a 6-level classification system and fine-tuned with just 
a few labeled examples. By leveraging the adaptability of LLMs, we can 
generate regulated descriptions for any level of detail with no additional
training required. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on both 
the existing and newly created datasets.

Causal analysis has long been a cornerstone of economic theory, with
Hicks and Marshall's concept of "marginal productivity" dating back to 1932.
Building on this foundation, Griliches and Brown (1961) and Griliches (1957)
further developed the "production function" approach to analyze a specific
input's contribution to production, known as an input's "marginal product."
In this context, "marginal product" is defined as the additional output
generated when an input is increased by one unit, with other factors held
constant.

In this study, "marginal product" is redefined using a new framework,
involving a production function that relates output to multiple inputs.
By applying a graphical model to depict the production function, "marginal
product" can be understood as the impact an input has on output when the
input is increased by one unit, with other factors and potential confounding
variables controlled for.

A graphical model is proposed to depict the production function, allowing
for the identification of "marginal product" as the impact an input has on
output when the input is increased by one unit, with other factors and
potential confounding variables controlled for. This new framework is
consistent with the earlier definitions of "marginal product" proposed by
Griliches and Hicks and Marshall.

This study introduces MMLSpark, an open-source Apache Spark library that integrates Spark SQL and ML with Microsoft's PyTorch for deep learning. The hybrid cloud architecture of Spark and PyTorch enables the development of PyTorch models distributed across multiple nodes. The MMLSpark innovation lies in its ability to integrate Spark's ML and SQL with PyTorch seamlessly. The core components of MMLSpark include the EmbeddingEngine, DistributedMLlib, and the Scaler, all built upon the PyTorch framework. The EmbeddingEngine facilitates the efficient transfer of data from Spark to PyTorch, while DistributedMLlib and Scaler enable the distributed training and data standardization respectively. The proposed approach is demonstrated through the Keras2PyTorch converter and the ImageNet classification example.

Voice translation faces a significant challenge in speaker identification, as speakers have not typically provided examples of themselves during training.  To address this issue, our research introduces a novel framework for voice synthesis and translation that achieves zero-shot performance on new speakers, speakers who have not been encountered before.  By integrating two key techniques, we are able to successfully implement this approach.  Firstly, we developed a speaker-agnostic voice model that can generate multiple voices from a single set of parameters.  Secondly, we designed a specialized voice selection module that can identify the most suitable voice for each speaker based on limited reference samples.  Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, as it outperforms existing methods in voice translation tasks.

We examine the solvability of a non-linear parabolic system, consisting of a heat equation in the interior of a fixed domain and a heat equation on the boundary, linked by non-linear relations that incorporate stress and inertia terms. These equations are analogous to the model introduced by Coleman and Gurtin in 1982, which is designed to model the movement of a surface within a heat-conducting solid. The model is subject to non-local constraints on the surface movement, and the movement is further restricted by a friction term proportional to the surface velocity. The model is studied on a fixed, sufficiently regular bounded domain in n-dimensional space, and the temperature is assumed to be positive, as per the absolute temperature scale proposed by Noll. The existence and uniqueness of a solution to the model are proven under suitable regularity assumptions. The key tools used in the proof are the theory of monotone operators and fixed point arguments.

Accurate short-term forecasts of aggregated low-voltage consumer electricity usage are crucial for managing the dynamic grid, particularly in areas with high shares of renewable energy. This study proposes a novel approach to probabilistic load forecasting, which leverages the benefits of combining forecasts from multiple models. By integrating the predictive capabilities of a Gaussian process and a deep learning-based autoregressive model, the ensemble method demonstrates superior performance compared to its individual components, as evidenced by experimental results. Furthermore, the developed approach enables the estimation of the probability of exceeding daily load thresholds, a useful tool for load management.

The increasing adoption of machine learning in healthcare and pharmaceutical sciences is being hampered by the difficulty of integrating valuable expert knowledge into the process. This review aims to provide a comprehensive overview of methods used to incorporate domain expertise into machine learning models, focusing on drug discovery and personalized medicine. These methods are categorized into three main approaches: (1) using domain expertise to guide the training process, (2) employing domain expertise to enhance data quality, and (3) leveraging domain expertise within neural network architectures. By dissecting the various integration techniques and highlighting their respective benefits and limitations, this work seeks to establish a unified framework for future research and development.

The COVID-19 dataset has gained significant attention due to the ongoing pandemic, presenting unique challenges in medical imaging. A major issue with current COVID-19 chest CT scan analysis is the lack of diversity in the data, leading to biased models that struggle with generalization. To address this problem, we propose a novel weakly guided learning approach that employs data augmentation to create a more diverse and representative dataset. By training on this enhanced dataset, our method effectively improves the accuracy of lesion detection and segmentation in CT scans. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of our approach over state-of-the-art methods.

The accurate identification of vertebrae in spine CT scans is a crucial task in radiology, yet it poses significant challenges due to the intricate nature of the spine, variations in image quality, and potential errors in conventional methods. To address these issues, a new, fully automated approach has been developed, which involves a two-stage process: first, the spine is straightened out using a flexible model, and then a precise search is conducted to isolate individual vertebrae. This method leverages the unique anatomical structure of the spine to guide the segmentation process, ensuring that vertebrae are accurately localized and labeled according to their anatomical position. By combining these techniques, this approach achieves a high level of accuracy, with segmentations that closely match those produced by experienced radiologists, as demonstrated through comprehensive evaluations using publicly available datasets.

Our research examines the impact of vacuum fluctuations on electron scattering from an atom in a ultrastrongly coupled cavity. When a continuous wave x-ray beam targets a cavity containing a few strongly interacting atoms, we find that the atoms' energy levels split into distinct peaks, and only certain gaps match the x-ray frequency. This phenomenon leads to a modified reflection pattern, and under certain conditions, it can be used to study strong light-matter interactions. Furthermore, we find that increased vacuum fluctuations enhance the effect, and higher temperatures can counteract it. This study provides a potential pathway to dynamically stabilize systems that would otherwise be unstable due to vacuum fluctuations.

A cutting-edge type of actuator, known as elastic actuators, has been developed and is gaining popularity in humanoid and quadrupedal robots. These actuators, which combine the benefits of traditional DC motors and biological muscle properties, can enhance a robot's natural appearance and performance. A significant challenge lies in adapting existing motor control methods to work with these new actuators. To address this issue, we've developed a novel elastic-actuated quadruped robot and introduced an innovative approach that leverages this new actuator type to improve the locomotion of the robot. This soft-actuated quadruped features compliant legs and specially designed springs to provide actuated ankle joints, giving it a natural, animal-like gait. To control the robot, we've developed an elastic-actuated model predictive controller that incorporates the robot's unique dynamics and spring characteristics. Experimental results show that our approach successfully enables the quadruped to walk and run, with the added benefit of increased stability and resilience to disturbances due to the robot's natural compliance.

The problem of distinguishing between two quantum states is significant in the fields of quantum information and quantum computing. We propose a novel approach that uses a variational method to measure the distinguishability of two quantum states. This method is based on a differential operator whose ground state energy corresponds to the distinguishability of the input states. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach with two examples, showing that it can be used to calculate the discrimination capability of any pair of states.

In a collisionless plasma, the tearing instability is triggered by the interaction of electrons and ions, resulting in the formation of electron diffusion regions. This process is studied in a specific regime where magnetic reconnection occurs at a scale comparable to the Larmor radius, and electron pressure effects are significant, but kinetic scales are much larger than the skin depth. A new model is proposed that combines fluid ion dynamics with kinetic electron behavior, and demonstrates that the tearing instability is driven by a specific current profile, and that the growth rate is influenced by the balance between magnetic and pressure forces, and electron dynamics. This model provides a deeper understanding of the role of kinetic effects in the tearing instability and its impact on magnetic reconnection.

The growing popularity of fashion e-commerce has led to a pressing need for efficient visual search functionality. Traditional approaches to visual search typically rely on a predefined set of query images, but this is often insufficient for users seeking specific styles. To address this, researchers have explored a more interactive method where users can adjust style attributes to refine their search. However, this interactive technique has a major limitation: it requires a large number of labeled data points, which is impractical to obtain. To overcome this challenge, we propose a new method that leverages a smaller amount of labeled data to learn the relationships between attributes and features, using a semi-supervised approach. By doing so, we can effectively handle attribute adjustments and improve the overall performance of visual search systems, even with limited labeled data.

We suggest and analyze two novel dual-based gradient algorithms for tackling linear ill-posed problems with convex regularization. The first method, called dual gradient descent, utilizes dual space elements to track the regularized solution, whereas the second method, called strong dual gradient descent, is able to track this solution with a better rate. The convergence of both algorithms is proven under the assumption that the regularizer is strongly convex, whereas in the case of weakly convex regularization, we show the existence of $\varepsilon$-solutions and prove the convergence of a variant of the strong dual gradient method. The key to these proofs lies in a dual-based version of dual regularity, a property that can be derived from primal space dual regularity for a broad range of regularizers. The effectiveness of the strong dual gradient method is demonstrated through a numerical example involving the deconvolution problem.

This research introduces a pioneering system for generating synthetic data at various spatial depths from multi-view images, specifically light field captures. The proposed OEC system mimics the effects of physical objects obstructing light, enabling training of depth estimation algorithms that are resilient to occlusions found in real-world light field depth estimation. Evaluations demonstrate that OEC-trained models significantly outperform those trained using conventional RGB data in terms of accuracy and robustness, achieving substantial gains in metric scores such as SSIM, RMSE, and Briseis.
The bilinear approach is employed to demonstrate the equivalence between the two Fokas-Lenells equations derived through the modern inverse scattering technique outlined by Fokas and Lenells in 2007.

We've discovered actions in double field theory that correspond to non-Riemannian gravitational theories, derived from the Heterotic and type I string theories, with no need for flux terms, in contrast to previously reported findings. These new actions, conforming to the doubled Poisson-Lie sigma model framework, yield a non-Riemannian gravitational action that deviates from standard Einstein-Hilbert action, particularly when expressed in conventional half-string form. This novel action exhibits explicit dependence on the double scalar sector and presents a unique non-Riemannian gravitational action, with action's behavior being invariant under generalized diffeomorphisms, thereby fulfilling a fundamental requirement.

In densely populated indoor environments with numerous wireless access points, selecting an optimal access point to connect to is a challenging task for mobile devices, particularly when multiple access points share the same network. This problem is compounded by devices often connecting to the nearest access point, disregarding its capacity and user load. Our solution, referred to as CEL, utilizes IEEE 802.11k/v standards to enable APs and extenders to report their capabilities and associated AP/Extender capabilities. By utilizing this information, our CEL approach allows devices to intelligently select an access point or extender that best suits their needs, thereby reducing network congestion and enhancing overall performance. Our CEL implementation has been successfully tested on real-world networks, demonstrating its effectiveness in improving network efficiency and reducing latency.
